passage:
Supervisor's note, internship programme, 30 June.
Ujjwal, one of our summer interns, puzzles me. He walks two kilometres from the station every morning in the heat to save the auto fare, and he refuses the canteen tea because it costs ten rupees. Yet last week, when the joining bonus arrived, he bought an expensive smartwatch the same afternoon. Vikas, the other intern, mentioned that Ujjwal is short for the hostel deposit due next week. When I asked Ujjwal about it gently, he said, "The bonus was extra. It didn't feel like my real money." He saw the problem as soon as he said it out loud. I didn't lecture. I suggested he list everything coming in and going out this month on one page, and offered him time with our finance officer if he wanted help.

qa.q: How far does Ujjwal walk from the station every morning?
qa.a: He walks two kilometres.

qa.q: Why did the bonus feel fine to spend on a smartwatch?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt happy and relaxed about the bonus as extra, not 'real money', so spending it seemed harmless, while daily costs felt serious enough to pinch.

qa.q: What did the supervisor suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Listing everything coming in and going out on one page, with time offered with the finance officer, so Ujjwal sees the whole picture instead of separate pots.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel about knowing Ujjwal is short for the deposit?
qa.a: Vikas might feel worried for Ujjwal and a little awkward about mentioning it.

grounding: Shows a student pinching on daily costs while spending a bonus at once, because separate mental pots hide the whole picture.

passage:
Wednesday
The college refunded my extra exam fee today: 6,000 rupees! It felt like a gift from the sky, so I booked the Goa trip with Nilesh and the others right away. No second thought.
This evening at the mess I skipped the extra paneer because it's twenty rupees. I've been skipping it all month. I also walked to the market instead of taking the bus, to save fifteen.
Nilesh noticed and laughed. "You'll spend six thousand in a minute and fight over twenty?" I told him the refund was a separate thing. Bonus money. Then he asked what my rent is next month, and whether I have it. I said... not yet.
I think my brain keeps different piggy banks and never adds them up. Tomorrow I'll sit down with Papa on the phone and look at all of it together.
Jeevan

qa.q: How much did the college refund Jeevan?
qa.a: 6,000 rupees.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan book the trip without a second thought?
qa.a: Jeevan felt thrilled and carefree, treating the refund as a gift from the sky, a separate pot from the everyday money being pinched.

qa.q: What is Jeevan planning, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Looking at all the money together with Papa on the phone, so rent, the trip and daily costs are seen as one picture.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see Jeevan's spending?
qa.a: Nilesh finds it funny and odd that Jeevan spends six thousand in a minute but fights over twenty.

grounding: Shows a student spending a refund at once while pinching tiny daily costs, missing the whole picture.

passage: When I got my first proper salary, I had money in five places and no idea what I owned. I'm Mahima. There was the savings account from college, a fixed deposit Papa had started, cash in an envelope, my salary account, and a wallet app. Each felt like a different kind of money. So I made one page, updated on the first Sunday of every month: everything I have, everything I owe, what came in, what went out. One number at the bottom. That page changed how I saw things. I still keep a separate 'Kerala trip' account, but only as a label for a goal, not as magic money. When my friend Pradeep asked how I'd saved for the trip while paying off my scooter, I showed him the page. He copied it that night.

qa.q: When does Mahima update the one page?
qa.a: On the first Sunday of every month.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about the money before making the page?
qa.a: Mahima felt confused and scattered, with money in five places and no clear sense of what was owned.

qa.q: What role does the 'Kerala trip' account play in Mahima's system?
qa.a: It's a label for a goal inside the whole picture, a helpful tool rather than a separate pot of magic money.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep have copied the page that night?
qa.a: Pradeep was probably impressed and curious, seeing how one clear page made saving for a trip and paying off a scooter fit together.

grounding: Shows a young earner treating all money as one picture, tracking it monthly, and using a labelled account only as a goal tool.

passage:
Mentor's note, 12 January.
I asked Lakshmi, who joined us two years ago, to talk to the new graduates about their first salaries, since hers is the calmest desk in the office. Pooja, one of the new joiners, said she keeps her bonus in a 'fun' account and her salary in a 'serious' one. Lakshmi smiled. "I used to do that too. Then I'd pinch every rupee on lunch while blowing the bonus on shoes." She showed them her single sheet: all accounts added together, debts taken away, money in and money out for the month. "The labels are still there," she said. "Rent, emergencies, my sister's wedding. But it's all one pool. I just look at the whole thing once a month." Pooja asked for a blank copy. I've asked HR to arrange a session with a certified financial adviser next month for anyone who wants it.

qa.q: What does Pooja keep in a 'fun' account?
qa.a: Pooja keeps her bonus in a 'fun' account.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi smile when Pooja describes her two accounts?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels amused and understanding, recognising her own old habit of pinching on lunch while spending the bonus on shoes.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi's single sheet do that separate accounts don't?
qa.a: It adds all accounts together and takes away debts, showing the whole pool and the month's flow, while labels remain as tools for goals.

qa.q: What might Pooja be feeling when she asks for a blank copy?
qa.a: Pooja seems curious and a little relieved to find a simpler way to see her first salary clearly.

grounding: Shows a young earner treating all money as one pool, tracking the whole picture monthly and using labels only as tools.

passage:
1 March
Monthly money check done. Took twenty minutes with chai. One sheet: savings, the small fund Dad helped me start, what I still owe on the laptop, salary in, spending out. Net: up a little from February. That tiny arrow going up is my favourite thing all month.
Ojas called while I was doing it and asked why I bother, since I 'keep the bonus separate anyway'. I told him I used to. The bonus felt like play money, and I'd spend it in a week while counting every rupee on groceries. Now it all goes on the same sheet. I still label one chunk 'Ladakh trip' so I can see it growing, but it's the same money, just with a name.
Next month the laptop will be fully paid off. Circled it.
Yash

qa.q: What does Yash still owe money on?
qa.a: Yash still owes money on the laptop.

qa.q: What does Yash feel when the net number goes up?
qa.a: Yash feels quietly pleased and satisfied; the tiny arrow going up is the favourite thing all month.

qa.q: How does Yash use the 'Ladakh trip' label differently from the old 'play money' bonus?
qa.a: It's a name for part of the same pool, so the trip can be seen growing, rather than a separate pot spent carelessly.

qa.q: Why might Ojas question the monthly check?
qa.a: Ojas still thinks of the bonus as separate, so a single sheet may seem like extra effort.

grounding: Shows a young earner tracking all money on one sheet each month and using a labelled goal as a tool, not a separate pot.

passage: In Durban, Zanele's mother called after her as she headed to the corner shop: "Bread, milk, two onions, the matches, not the big box, ask Mr Tuan if the gas man came, bring the change, and don't forget the eggs!" Zanele nodded and ran. At the counter, Mr Tuan waited. "Bread," Zanele said. "And... milk." Then nothing. Her head felt like a sieve. Onions? Something about gas? She walked home with bread and milk and a worried face. Her mother laughed, not crossly, and tore a page from a notebook. "Too many at once. My mistake." Next time she gave Zanele three things, then sent her back for three more. Zanele came home with everything, and the right change.

qa.q: What did Zanele remember to buy?
qa.a: Bread and milk.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel standing at the counter?
qa.a: Zanele felt flustered and worried, her head like a sieve, because too many instructions had come at once.

qa.q: What did Zanele's mother change, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gave three things at a time, which fits what a child's memory can hold.

qa.q: How did Zanele's mother see the mix-up?
qa.a: She laughed kindly and took the blame, seeing the list as too long rather than Zanele as careless.

grounding: Shows a child forgetting most of a long list of errands and managing well once given a few at a time.

passage: In the Class 6 science lab, Aparna ma'am rattled off the instructions: "Put on goggles, take the blue beaker, fill it halfway, add two spoons of salt, stir twenty times, label it with your name, put it on the windowsill, and wash your spoon." Mridul nodded along. Then he stood at the bench and his mind went blank. He filled the beaker to the top, forgot the salt, and put it on the windowsill without a label. Half the class had done something similar. Aparna ma'am looked at the row of unlabelled beakers and sighed, then smiled. "Too many steps at once." The next week she wrote three steps on the board, waited, then wrote the next three. Mridul finished first and even remembered to wash his spoon.

qa.q: What colour was the beaker?
qa.a: The beaker was blue.

qa.q: Why did Mridul's mind go blank at the bench?
qa.a: Mridul felt confused and overwhelmed, because eight steps said all at once were more than he could hold in his head.

qa.q: What did Aparna ma'am change the next week, and why did it help?
qa.a: She wrote three steps on the board at a time, giving the class short, clear steps that memory can hold.

qa.q: How did Aparna ma'am see the row of unlabelled beakers?
qa.a: She sighed, then smiled, recognising that the problem was too many steps at once, not careless children.

grounding: Shows a child forgetting most of a long spoken lab instruction, and doing well once steps are given a few at a time.

passage:
Saturday. Samir gave his daughter Charu the whole recipe for masala chai at once: water, ginger, crushed cardamom, boil, tea leaves, milk, sugar, boil again, lower the flame, strain. Charu, ten, started well, then forgot the tea leaves and let the milk boil over.
Sunday. They tried again. This time Samir said only, "Water, ginger, cardamom. Boil." When it bubbled, he gave the next three. Charu nodded at each small set.
The next Saturday. Charu stuck a card on the fridge with the steps in four short lines, and made chai for the whole family by herself. Samir sipped it and said it was better than his. Charu said it was because she had the card.

qa.q: What did Charu forget on the first Saturday?
qa.a: She forgot the tea leaves.

qa.q: What does Charu's nodding at each small set suggest on Sunday?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calmer and more confident, because three steps at a time were easy to hold in mind.

qa.q: Why did the card on the fridge work so well?
qa.a: Four short lines kept the steps outside her head, so her memory didn't have to hold the whole recipe at once.

qa.q: How did Samir feel sipping the chai the next Saturday?
qa.a: Samir felt proud and pleased, saying it was better than his.

grounding: Shows a child forgetting parts of a long recipe given all at once, and succeeding with a few short steps at a time.

passage: Last term I thought I was studying for three hours a night. I'm Lalit. My desk had my history book, my phone, and a playlist of my favourite songs, the ones I sing along to. Every few minutes the phone buzzed: the class group, a cricket score, a meme. I'd reply, read a line, hum a chorus, read another line. In the test I couldn't remember a single date from the chapter I'd 'studied' four times. My sister Sangeeta watched me one evening and said, "You read the same paragraph five times. I counted." So I tried her way: phone in the kitchen, music without words, forty minutes, then a break. Honestly, it felt boring at first. But the next week I could explain the whole chapter to her without the book.

qa.q: Where did Lalit put the phone when trying Sangeeta's way?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel during the test, and why?
qa.a: Lalit felt shocked and frustrated, unable to remember a single date, because the buzzing phone and singing along had kept the chapter from sticking.

qa.q: Which parts of Sangeeta's way helped the chapter stick?
qa.a: Phone in another room, music without words, and forty-minute blocks with breaks, so attention wasn't split.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta notice while watching Lalit study?
qa.a: Sangeeta noticed Lalit reading the same paragraph five times, and counted to prove it.

grounding: Shows a teenager studying with a buzzing phone and lyric songs and finding nothing sticks until the distractions are removed.

passage:
Tuition centre note, Tuesday evening.
Gautam sat at the back again with one earphone in and his phone face up beside his notebook. In the hour I watched, it lit up eleven times. Each time he glanced at it, and each time he lost his place in the quadratic equations. When I asked him to explain the method afterwards, he couldn't. "But I was listening," he said, surprised at himself. Darshan, next to him, whose phone stays in his bag, explained it clearly. I didn't take Gautam's phone away. I asked him to try tomorrow with it switched off inside his bag and no music, just for one hour, and to notice the difference himself. I've also told his mother about the plan, so home study can try the same.

qa.q: How many times did Gautam's phone light up in the hour?
qa.a: It lit up eleven times.

qa.q: Why was Gautam surprised when he couldn't explain the method?
qa.a: Gautam felt sure he had been listening, so he was surprised and a bit embarrassed to find the buzzing phone and music had kept the method from sticking.

qa.q: What did the teacher suggest, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: One hour with the phone off in his bag and no music, so Gautam can notice the difference himself instead of being forced.

qa.q: How might Darshan's experience of the lesson differ?
qa.a: With the phone in the bag, Darshan could follow the equations and explain them clearly.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose buzzing phone and music keep a maths method from sticking in a study session.

passage:
Thursday
Did an experiment for Chaitanya's bet. Yesterday: biology chapter with the phone next to me and my usual songs. Today: a chapter of the same length, phone in Mummy's cupboard, no songs, just the fan.
Results. Yesterday I read for two hours, answered about thirty messages, and could recall maybe four facts. Today I read for one hour and could draw the whole heart diagram from memory, arrows and all. Annoying.
Chaitanya said songs with words are the worst because your brain tries to follow them too. I said my brain is a genius and can do both. Clearly it can't.
I felt jittery for the first twenty minutes without the phone, like it was calling me from the cupboard. Then my head went quiet. Tomorrow: chemistry, cupboard again.
Suraj

qa.q: Where did Suraj put the phone today?
qa.a: In Mummy's cupboard.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel in the first twenty minutes without the phone?
qa.a: Suraj felt jittery, as if the phone was calling from the cupboard, until things went quiet.

qa.q: What did the experiment show, and what is Suraj's next step?
qa.a: One focused hour without phone or lyrics beat two distracted hours; Suraj plans chemistry tomorrow with the phone in the cupboard again.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya explain why songs with words are the worst?
qa.a: Chaitanya says the brain tries to follow the lyrics too, so attention is split.

grounding: Shows a teenager finding that studying with a phone and lyric songs made little stick, compared with a quiet hour.

passage: The week before her final exams, Himani was doing night shifts at the café to cover her rent, and her mother had been admitted to hospital back home in Nagpur. On Thursday the power went out in the hostel, and she studied by phone torch until the battery died. On Friday, at the café, she gave a customer change for a five-hundred note when he had paid with a hundred. Then she sent Varun her exam timetable with Tuesday written as Wednesday. He caught it. "You never make mistakes like this," he said on the phone. Himani sat on the café's back step. Her head felt full of cotton. "I'm not stupid," she said. "I'm just carrying too much." Varun offered to swap his Saturday shift with hers so she could sleep and call home.

qa.q: What did Himani write wrongly on the timetable?
qa.a: She wrote Tuesday as Wednesday.

qa.q: How did Himani feel sitting on the café's back step?
qa.a: Himani felt foggy and overwhelmed, her head full of cotton, knowing the mistakes came from carrying too much at once.

qa.q: What did Varun offer, and why does it help?
qa.a: Swapping his Saturday shift so she could sleep and call home, which takes some load off so her mind has more room.

qa.q: Why was Varun surprised by the mistakes?
qa.a: Varun knows Himani never makes mistakes like this, so he sensed something was wrong.

grounding: Shows a student juggling exams, work and worry about her mother making careless mistakes and feeling foggy.

passage: In the week of his semester exams, Asif was also delivering food on his scooter every evening in Hyderabad, and his parents were arguing on the phone about his younger brother's school fees. On Monday he locked himself out of the room twice. On Tuesday he submitted his lab report with last year's file attached. On Wednesday he walked into the wrong exam hall and sat down before someone asked for his hall ticket. That night Pranav found him staring into the fridge, holding the milk and a pen, unsure why he had either. "Bro, you're running on empty," Pranav said. Asif laughed, then his eyes stung. "I'm not careless. I'm just full." They sat on the floor and wrote everything on one page: exams, shifts, the home stuff. Asif took Thursday off deliveries and emailed the professor about the report.

qa.q: What did Asif attach to his lab report by mistake?
qa.a: He attached last year's file.

qa.q: What did Asif mean by 'I'm not careless. I'm just full'?
qa.a: Asif felt exhausted and overwhelmed, and knew the mistakes came from too many things filling his mind, not from not caring.

qa.q: What did Asif and Pranav do, and why does it help?
qa.a: They wrote everything on one page, and Asif took Thursday off deliveries and emailed the professor, which lightens the load and fixes one mistake.

qa.q: How did Pranav read Asif at the fridge?
qa.a: Pranav saw someone running on empty, not being silly, and gently named it.

grounding: Shows a student juggling exams, work and family worries making careless mistakes and feeling foggy.

passage:
"Jaya, you've written 'total' as 'totla' three times."
"Have I?" Jaya stared at the page. "Pranav, I don't even know what I'm doing. I've got the audit exam Monday, my internship report due Tuesday, and Amma called to say the landlord's raising the rent."
"Okay."
"And I got the balance sheet wrong. Twice. I've done this a hundred times."
"Because you're doing four things in your head at once."
"I'm just being stupid."
"You're not stupid. You're full." Pranav pulled out a sheet of paper. "Write it all down. Every worry. Then we pick one."
She wrote: exam, report, rent, sleep.
"Now, which one is today?"
"The exam."
"Then the rest waits on the paper." He tapped it. "Do one balance sheet. Slowly."
Her third try balanced.

qa.q: How did Jaya misspell 'total'?
qa.a: She wrote it as 'totla'.

qa.q: Why does Jaya think she's 'just being stupid'?
qa.a: Jaya feels frustrated and ashamed at getting a familiar balance sheet wrong, not seeing that the exam, the report and the rent worry are crowding her mind.

qa.q: What did Pranav suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing every worry on paper and picking one for today, which frees up her mind so the balance sheet finally balances.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Jaya's mistakes?
qa.a: Pranav sees a friend who is full, not stupid, and helps her put the worries down.

grounding: Shows a student juggling an exam, a report and a rent worry making careless mistakes until the load is put on paper.

passage: Three days before the Bhatt wedding, Avni, the event manager, had forty-two things in her head, and the caterer had just cancelled. Her phone buzzed every few seconds: the family group, the decorators' group, the band, her own mother. She felt her thoughts start to scatter. So she stopped. She muted every group except the bride's father. She took a fresh sheet and wrote down everything, all forty-two, then split the biggest one, 'find new caterer', into steps: call three backups, taste on Wednesday, confirm by Thursday noon. She handed Arohi, her assistant, eleven items. Then she walked round the block for ten minutes without her phone. When she came back, the list looked like jobs, not a storm. By Thursday noon, the new caterer was signed.

qa.q: How many things did Avni write down?
qa.a: She wrote down all forty-two.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when her thoughts started to scatter, and what did she do?
qa.a: Avni felt overwhelmed by the cancelled caterer and the constant buzzing, and chose to stop and lighten the load instead of pushing on.

qa.q: Which of Avni's steps made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Writing everything down and breaking 'find new caterer' into three steps, which turned a storm of worries into clear jobs.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel getting eleven items?
qa.a: Arohi might feel trusted and busy, and relieved to have clear tasks rather than chaos.

grounding: Shows a young event manager writing everything down, splitting a big job into steps, muting groups and taking a break under time pressure.

passage: At her desk on the sixth floor in Gurugram, Amandeep used to keep fourteen tabs open, two chat apps pinging, and a sticky note of 'urgent' things curling at the edges. By five she was always exhausted and had finished almost nothing. In January she changed three things. Every morning she wrote the day's work on paper, breaking each big task into steps small enough to finish in an hour. She turned off every notification except direct messages from her team lead. And every ninety minutes she walked to the window and back, leaving her phone behind. Deepak, at the next desk, noticed in February. "You've stopped sighing," he said. "And you shipped the payment feature early." Amandeep laughed. "My brain just has room now."

qa.q: Which notifications did Amandeep keep on?
qa.a: Only direct messages from her team lead.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel at five o'clock before January?
qa.a: Amandeep felt exhausted and frustrated, having finished almost nothing despite a full day.

qa.q: Which of Amandeep's changes could someone else try tomorrow?
qa.a: Writing the day's work on paper in hour-sized steps, turning off needless notifications, and taking a short walk every ninety minutes.

qa.q: What did Deepak notice about Amandeep in February?
qa.a: Deepak noticed she had stopped sighing and had shipped the payment feature early.

grounding: Shows a young developer writing tasks down, splitting them into steps, cutting notifications and taking breaks so her mind can focus.

passage:
"How are you so calm, Kiran? You teach five classes and run the science club."
"I'm not calm by nature. I just stopped trusting my head to hold everything."
"Meaning?"
Kiran opened a small notebook. "Everything goes in here. Marking, parent calls, club stuff. If it's written, I don't have to keep remembering it."
"And the huge things? Like the annual exhibition?"
"Broken into bits. This week it's only 'book the hall'. Next week, 'list the projects'."
"My phone buzzes all day with school groups."
"Mine too. I turned them off. I check them twice a day, at lunch and at four."
Anjali sighed. "And breaks?"
"Ten minutes after every two classes. I sit outside. No phone."
"That sounds too simple."
"It is simple. That's why it works."

qa.q: When does Kiran check the school groups?
qa.a: Twice a day, at lunch and at four.

qa.q: Why did Kiran stop 'trusting my head to hold everything'?
qa.a: Kiran felt overwhelmed trying to remember everything, and found calm by moving tasks into a notebook.

qa.q: Which of Kiran's habits could help Anjali most, and why?
qa.a: Writing everything down and breaking big projects into weekly bits, because it frees the mind to focus on one thing at a time.

qa.q: How does Anjali seem to feel during the conversation?
qa.a: Anjali seems overwhelmed and a little doubtful, sighing and finding it all too simple.

grounding: Shows a young teacher lightening mental load by writing things down, splitting big jobs, cutting notifications and taking breaks.

passage: On Ankita's first day at the bank branch in Nashik, the manager handed her a 200-page procedures manual and three login passwords and told her to shadow the counter. By noon, Aditi, two years senior, noticed Ankita staring at the same page, pen still, eyes glassy. At lunch Aditi sat beside her. "Too much?" Ankita nodded, embarrassed. "I've read forty pages and I remember nothing." Aditi took the manual and closed it. "Forget this for now. This week, only three things: opening the counter, cash deposits and passbook updates." She wrote a short checklist for each, walked Ankita through two real deposits, and let her do the third while she watched. By Friday, Ankita ran the deposit counter alone for an hour. Next week: withdrawals.

qa.q: How many pages long was the procedures manual?
qa.a: It was 200 pages long.

qa.q: What did Aditi notice and feel when she saw Ankita at noon?
qa.a: Aditi felt concerned, noticing Ankita staring at the same page with glassy eyes, clearly drowning in information.

qa.q: Which of Aditi's steps made the difference for Ankita?
qa.a: Limiting the week to three things, writing short checklists, showing real examples and letting Ankita practise while being watched.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel at lunch on the first day?
qa.a: Ankita felt embarrassed and overwhelmed, having read forty pages and remembered nothing.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague noticing a new hire overwhelmed and giving information in small stages with examples, checklists and practice.

passage:
Hi Ritu,
A quick note about Mohit, our new trainee. I've been sitting near him this week, and I think we're drowning him. On day one he got the style guide, the client list, four software tools and the whole project history. Yesterday I saw him reread the same email for ten minutes, and he admitted he'd forgotten the client's name during a call. He's clearly sharp; it's just too much at once.
Could we try this instead? Week one: only the Sharma account, with one example report that I'll walk him through, and a one-page checklist for the reporting tool. Week two: he writes a report himself and I review it. Only then do we add the other clients.
I'm happy to own this. I remember my own first week here. I thought I was stupid for a month.
Vijay

qa.q: Which account does Vijay suggest Mohit start with?
qa.a: The Sharma account.

qa.q: What does Vijay feel watching Mohit this week?
qa.a: Vijay feels concerned and sympathetic, remembering feeling stupid in that first month, and sees Mohit is overwhelmed, not slow.

qa.q: What does Vijay's plan do to lighten Mohit's load?
qa.a: It stages the learning: one account, one worked example, a one-page checklist, then practice with review before adding more.

qa.q: What might Mohit's first week have felt like?
qa.a: Mohit probably felt flooded and embarrassed, rereading emails and forgetting a client's name despite being sharp.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague noticing a new trainee overwhelmed and proposing information in small stages with an example, a checklist and practice.

passage: People ask how I train new cooks, so let me tell you about Rehana. I'm Samir, the sous-chef at a small restaurant in Kochi. Rehana joined last spring, and on her first night the head chef shouted forty instructions across a full kitchen. By nine she had burnt two pans and was crying in the store room. I recognised the look: not lazy, just flooded. The next day I changed things. One station only, the salad counter. I showed her three dishes, one at a time, and taped a small card above her board with each step. She practised in the quiet hour before service. After a week we added the grill, with a card for that too. By autumn she was running the whole cold kitchen. The cards are still up. New cooks use them now.

qa.q: Which station did Samir start Rehana on?
qa.a: The salad counter.

qa.q: What did Samir feel on seeing Rehana in the store room?
qa.a: Samir felt sympathetic, recognising that she was flooded with instructions, not lazy.

qa.q: Which parts of Samir's training helped Rehana most?
qa.a: One station at a time, three dishes shown one by one, a step card above her board, and practice in the quiet hour.

qa.q: How did Rehana's first night feel for her?
qa.a: Rehana felt overwhelmed and upset, burning pans and ending up crying in the store room after forty shouted instructions.

grounding: Shows a senior cook noticing a new hire drowning in instructions and giving them in small stages with examples, cards and practice.

passage: In the courtyard in Karjat, two-year-old Nitin crouched over a row of pebbles, lining them up one by one. "Nitin! Bath time!" called Vandana from the doorway. He didn't look up. "Nitin!" Louder. Nothing. His tongue poked out as he placed the next pebble. Vandana walked over, knelt, and touched his shoulder. Nitin jumped, looked up, and smiled as if he had only just noticed her. "Mumma! Look!" He held up a pebble.

qa.q: What was Nitin lining up?
qa.a: A row of pebbles.

qa.q: Why didn't Nitin answer when Vandana called?
qa.a: Nitin felt so absorbed and content with the pebbles that her voice didn't reach his attention; it wasn't defiance.

qa.q: What worked for Vandana, and why?
qa.a: Kneeling and touching his shoulder, which gently pulled his attention from the pebbles to her.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt calling more than once?
qa.a: Vandana might have felt a little impatient at first, then realised he simply hadn't heard.

grounding: Shows a toddler so absorbed in pebbles that he doesn't hear his name, a normal attention limit rather than defiance.

passage: During Ramadan in Amman, the family gathered for iftar as the sun went down. Two-year-old Bilal sat under the window, watching a paper lantern turn slowly, throwing coloured shapes on the wall. "Bilal, come, habibi, dates!" called his mother, Yara. He didn't move. His grandmother called too. Nothing. His eyes followed a red star sliding across the wall. Yara picked up the plate of dates and sat beside him on the floor. When the lantern stopped, Bilal turned, saw the dates, and grinned.

qa.q: What was the lantern throwing on the wall?
qa.a: Coloured shapes.

qa.q: Why didn't Bilal come when Yara called?
qa.a: Bilal felt delighted and fascinated by the lantern's moving shapes, so absorbed that the calls didn't reach his attention; he wasn't ignoring them on purpose.

qa.q: What did Yara do that worked?
qa.a: She brought the dates and sat beside him, waiting until his attention was free instead of calling louder.

qa.q: How might Bilal's grandmother see him under the window?
qa.a: His grandmother might smile, seeing a little one lost in the lantern, not a naughty child.

grounding: Shows a toddler so absorbed in a turning lantern that he does not hear his name, a normal limit rather than defiance.

passage:
Monday, the first snow in Shimla. Karthik, two, stood with his nose on the window, watching the flakes. Kashish called, "Karthik, shoes on!" three times. He didn't turn. She felt a flash of irritation.
Wednesday. Karthik was stacking cups on the rug. Kashish called; nothing. Remembering Monday, she crouched in front of him until he saw her face.
Saturday. Before calling, Kashish touched his hand. Karthik looked up at once. "Snow?" he asked. "Snow," she said, and they went out together.

qa.q: What was Karthik watching on Monday?
qa.a: He was watching the snowflakes.

qa.q: Why didn't Karthik turn when Kashish called three times?
qa.a: Karthik felt entranced by the snow, so absorbed that her voice didn't break through; he wasn't being defiant.

qa.q: What did Kashish change by Saturday, and why did it work?
qa.a: She touched his hand before calling, which gently caught his attention first.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel on Monday compared with Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday Kashish felt a flash of irritation; by Saturday she was calmer, knowing how to reach him.

grounding: Shows a toddler too absorbed to hear his name, and a mother learning it is attention, not defiance.

passage:
Nursery class note, Friday.
We had a puppet show today: a crow and a fox arguing over a piece of cheese. Siddharth sat in the front row, mouth open. Halfway through, Vidya ma'am from the office walked right across the back of the stage carrying a tall stack of chairs and wearing a bright orange dupatta. Almost every child turned. Siddharth didn't blink. Afterwards, when the others giggled about the orange chair lady, Siddharth frowned. "What lady?" He insisted there had been no lady. I told him it's normal: when we watch one thing very hard, other things can disappear. He thought that was like magic.

qa.q: What were the crow and the fox arguing over?
qa.a: A piece of cheese.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth insist there had been no lady?
qa.a: Siddharth felt sure and puzzled, because he had been so absorbed in the puppets that Vidya ma'am never entered his attention.

qa.q: How did the teacher explain it, and why is that a helpful way to put it?
qa.a: The teacher said watching one thing hard can make other things disappear, which helps Siddharth see it as normal, not a mistake.

qa.q: How might the other children see Siddharth's 'What lady?'
qa.a: They might find it funny or surprising, since the orange dupatta and chairs seemed impossible to miss.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so fixed on a puppet show that he misses a person walking across the stage.

passage: At the village fair in Nagaur, the kathputli puppets danced on their strings while the drum beat fast. Raghav, five, sat on the dusty ground, eyes fixed on the puppet king waving his sword. His big sister Arohi, back from buying balloons, walked right in front of him holding three red ones, and even waved. Raghav didn't move. When the show ended, he jumped up. "Where's Arohi didi? She's been gone so long!" Arohi laughed and held out a balloon. "I walked past you! I waved!" Raghav's mouth fell open. "You did not." "I did." He looked at the empty stage, then back at her, and wondered how.

qa.q: What colour were the balloons Arohi carried?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why did Raghav think Arohi had been gone so long?
qa.a: Raghav felt surprised and a little worried, because he was so absorbed in the puppet king that he never saw her walk past and wave.

qa.q: What could help Raghav understand what happened?
qa.a: A grown-up could explain gently that when we watch one thing very closely, other things can pass unseen.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when Raghav said 'You did not'?
qa.a: Arohi was amused and laughed, knowing she had walked right in front of him.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so absorbed in a puppet show that he misses his sister walking past and waving.

passage: At the library in Oslo, Ulla, five, sat cross-legged in front of the puppet theatre, watching a clumsy troll try to bake a cake. She laughed so hard she hiccupped. While the troll dropped the eggs, a librarian in a big yellow raincoat pushed a squeaky book trolley right behind the theatre. Ulla's friend Nkechi pointed and whispered. Ulla didn't turn her head. After the show, Nkechi said, "Did you see the trolley? It squeaked so loud!" Ulla blinked. "What trolley?" She was sure there hadn't been one. They asked the librarian, who laughed and pointed at the trolley by the door.

qa.q: What was the troll trying to do?
qa.a: The troll was trying to bake a cake.

qa.q: Why was Ulla so sure there hadn't been a trolley?
qa.a: Ulla felt certain and surprised, because she was so absorbed in the troll that the squeaky trolley never reached her attention.

qa.q: What might a grown-up tell Ulla about this?
qa.a: That when we focus hard on one thing, our attention hides the rest, which is normal and even a bit funny.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Ulla said 'What trolley?'
qa.a: Nkechi might have felt puzzled and amused, since the trolley seemed so loud and obvious.

grounding: Shows a preschooler so fixed on a puppet show that a noisy trolley passing behind goes unnoticed.

passage: In the Class 6 science club, Rehana ma'am played a short video of students passing a basketball. "Count how many times the white-shirt team passes. Carefully." Gurleen leaned forward, lips moving. Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. When the video ended, she shot up her hand. "Fifteen!" "Correct," said Rehana ma'am. "And did anyone see the tiger?" Half the room burst out laughing. Gurleen frowned. What tiger? Rehana ma'am played it again. Right in the middle, a person in a tiger costume walked slowly through the players, waved at the camera and walked off. Gurleen's jaw dropped. "That wasn't there!" "It was," said Rehana ma'am. "Your eyes saw it. Your attention didn't."

qa.q: How many passes did Gurleen count?
qa.a: Fifteen.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen insist 'That wasn't there!'?
qa.a: Gurleen felt shocked and puzzled, because her attention was so fixed on counting passes that the tiger never registered.

qa.q: What does this experiment teach Gurleen about noticing things?
qa.a: That attention decides what we see, so when focused on one task, it helps to look again or ask others what they noticed.

qa.q: How might the children who saw the tiger feel?
qa.a: They probably felt amused and a bit proud, laughing that anyone could miss something so strange.

grounding: Shows a child counting passes in a video and missing a person in a tiger costume walking through.

passage:
Monday. Bhavna didi showed Hrithik a video on her phone. "Count the passes by the red team." Hrithik counted eleven, proudly. "And the man with the umbrella?" There was no man. She replayed it. A man with a big black umbrella strolled right through the middle. Hrithik felt his ears go hot.
Wednesday. Hrithik made his own version with his cricket friends: count the catches, while Pintu walked through wearing a bucket on his head. He showed Bhavna didi. She missed the bucket. He laughed for ten minutes.
Saturday. He tested Papa at dinner. Papa missed the bucket too. "It's not your eyes," Hrithik explained grandly. "It's where your attention goes."

qa.q: What did the man in didi's video carry?
qa.a: A big black umbrella.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel on Monday when the video was replayed?
qa.a: Hrithik felt embarrassed, his ears going hot, having been so focused on counting that he missed something obvious.

qa.q: What did Hrithik learn by making his own video?
qa.a: That almost anyone misses something surprising when focused on one task, so it's about attention, not bad eyes.

qa.q: How might Bhavna didi have felt missing the bucket on Wednesday?
qa.a: Bhavna didi was probably surprised and amused, and understood how Hrithik had felt on Monday.

grounding: Shows a child counting passes and missing a man with an umbrella, then discovering that others miss obvious things too.

passage: Ayesha, you missed the bus because you were counting stickers? Sit with your Noor nani. When I was nine, in Rampur, my Abba made me count mangoes at his fruit stall every evening. One day a new crate came. "A hundred and twenty," he said. "Check it." I counted so hard my lips moved. Eighty-one, eighty-two. A goat wandered right up to the stall, stood beside me and ate three mangoes off the top of the crate. The whole bazaar was laughing. I didn't see it. I finished, proudly: "One hundred and seventeen, Abba! Three missing!" Abba laughed till he cried. My friend Shabnam from the next stall said the goat had even bumped my elbow. I didn't believe her until I saw the goat, still chewing.

qa.q: How many mangoes did young Noor count?
qa.a: One hundred and seventeen.

qa.q: Why didn't young Noor see the goat eating the mangoes?
qa.a: Noor felt so focused and proud about counting correctly that her attention shut out the goat, even though it was right beside her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nani's story, and what does it show?
qa.a: Seeing the goat still chewing, which showed that attention decides what we see, not the eyes alone.

qa.q: How did Abba react to Noor's report of three missing mangoes?
qa.a: Abba laughed till he cried, having watched the goat eat them right beside her.

grounding: Shows a child so focused on counting mangoes that she doesn't notice a goat eating them beside her.
